projects.name: Cider making
projects.status: Three 7-gallon fermenters were pitched with M02 on Nov 15. The two plastic ones (17 Brix at the start) are fermenting well, have had their first Fermaid O and show no rotten-egg smell. The glass one (14 Brix at the start) was slow to start but is now bubbling steadily through the airlock, with little froth on the surface, which is normal for a cool cider ferment. The Jonagold cider pressed Oct 3 is in two full kegs and one half keg: good already, better with age. Some gets poured young at Thanksgiving and over the holidays, and the half keg is set aside for spicing. The keezer build comes after.

think.text: Would like the keezer built out before the end of the year. The picnic tap covers Thanksgiving in the meantime.
This yeast tends to throw sulfur at certain temperatures and when nitrogen is short, which is why the nutrient timing matters.
Aiming for about 65 F, but no spot in the house holds a steady temperature.
The open batch is taking on oxygen. If the tubing run slips, a blanket of CO2 from your tank over the surface buys some time.
16 gallons fills three 5-gallon kegs with about a gallon left over. Have a fourth keg or a smaller vessel ready.

A third of the way through is a third of the sugar gone. From 17 Brix that is about 11.5 Brix. From 14 Brix it is about 9.5 Brix. Those are hydrometer Brix; a refractometer would read about 13 and about 11 at the same points, because alcohol pushes its reading up.
A rotten-egg smell early on is the cue to add nutrient and hold the temperature steady. It is easier to prevent than to remove.
A picnic tap has a short line, so it foams at keg pressure. Vent the keg and pour at about 2 to 4 psi, then put it back to serving pressure afterward.
The half-full keg got a double sulfite dose for its volume. Pour a full keg at Thanksgiving and give the half keg 2 to 3 more weeks.

The glass fermenter was simply behind: glass in a cool room runs a couple of degrees under plastic and warms slowly. Bubbling can also come from a warming carboy, so a falling Brix reading is the real confirmation.
Contamination usually shows itself as a film on the surface or a vinegar or nail-polish smell. If it still smells like clean juice, that is good news.
Do not let dose 2 slip past the one-third point; the yeast take up less nutrient the further along they are.

refs.title: Racking day checklist, for next year
body: Buy food-grade tubing at the brew shop
Clean the corny kegs with PBW, rinse, and replace all the O-rings
Sanitize the kegs with Star San
Rack the 16-gallon batch straight into the kegs
Purge the headspace with CO2 and pressurize the kegs for long-term aging
Add 1/4 tsp potassium metabisulfite per 5 gallons at racking; halve it for a half-full keg
Full detail for each step is in Racking into kegs, in order

refs.title: Racking into kegs, in order
body: Confirm fermentation is done: the same reading three days apart, usually 0 Brix or just below on the hydrometer (a refractometer still shows about 4 to 6 Brix).
Release any pressure, then take each keg apart: lid, posts and dip tubes.
Soak or scrub everything in hot PBW, then rinse until the water runs clear. Never bleach.
Fit new O-rings on the lid, posts and dip tubes with a thin film of keg lube, and reassemble.
Leak test: pressurize to 30 psi, spray sanitizer on the lid and posts, and watch for bubbles.
Add Star San, seal, shake to coat every surface, then push it out through the liquid post with CO2. The keg is left sanitized and full of gas.
Run sanitizer through the siphon and the full length of the new tubing.
Dissolve 1/4 tsp (about 1.5 g) potassium metabisulfite per 5-gallon keg in 1/4 cup of boiled, cooled water and pour it into the empty keg.
Fermenter up high, keg on the floor. Give the keg a gentle stream of CO2 for 20 to 30 seconds just before filling.
Siphon from just above the sediment with the tube resting on the keg bottom so it fills without splashing. Stop an inch or two below the bottom of the gas dip tube.
Seal, pressurize to 30 psi and vent through the relief valve 5 or 6 times, then hold at 10 to 15 psi for aging.
Clean the 16-gallon fermenter the same day, before the yeast cake dries on.

refs.title: Keg pressures and force carbonation
body: All pressures assume a cold keg at fridge temperature, about 38 F. Chill first: cold cider takes up CO2 far better than warm.
Aging: purge the headspace (30 psi, vent 5 or 6 times), then hold at 10 to 15 psi. The keg can sit disconnected from the tank; it seals itself.
Aging at 20 psi is also safe. Kept cold for weeks it ends up near 3 volumes of CO2, which is very fizzy, so vent it and let it settle at serving pressure for a day or two before pouring.
Serving: 10 to 12 psi, roughly 2.5 volumes of CO2. For a champagne-like sparkle use 14 to 15 psi with about 10 feet of 3/16 inch beverage line to keep the foam down.
Carbonating, slow and safe: connect the gas at 10 to 12 psi and leave it 1 to 2 weeks. It cannot overshoot.
Carbonating, burst: 30 psi for 24 to 36 hours, then vent and drop to serving pressure. Drinkable in 2 to 3 days.
Carbonating, same day: at 30 psi, rock or roll the keg for a few minutes, rest it an hour or more, vent, then set serving pressure. Fast but easy to overdo.
Too fizzy: take the gas off, vent the relief valve a few times over a day, then reconnect at serving pressure.
After a party: top up to serving pressure, pull both disconnects and keep the keg cold. A month later, check that the relief valve still hisses; if not, find the leak.

refs.title: Nutrient plan for the 7-gallon fermenters
body: Yeast is Mangrove Jack's M02. Fermaid O only; Go-Ferm is for rehydrating yeast before pitching, so it is not used here.
Dose 1: 3 g Fermaid O per fermenter at the first signs of active fermentation.
Dose 2: 3 g Fermaid O per fermenter at one-third sugar depletion.
This batch: the two plastic fermenters started at 17 Brix, so dose 2 goes in at about 11.5 Brix. The glass fermenter started at 14 Brix, so its dose 2 goes in at about 9.5 Brix.
Finding the one-third point: take a Brix reading at dose 1 and treat it as the starting Brix. Target = starting Brix x 2/3. Examples: 12 to 8, 13.5 to 9, 15 to 10.

Once the airlock is bubbling steadily, check Brix daily until dose 2 is in; at 65 F the one-third point usually comes 4 to 6 days into active fermentation. Use the hydrometer's Brix scale; a refractometer reads high once alcohol is present (about 13 Brix instead of 11.5, and about 11 instead of 9.5, at the one-third point).
To add: weigh on a gram scale, stir into about 1/2 cup of cider or non-chlorinated water, pour in slowly and swirl gently so it does not foam over.
Rotten-egg smell: add 3 g more per fermenter, once. Do not add nutrient once the Brix has dropped past halfway.
Hold the fermenters at 60 to 65 F. Below about 55 F this yeast stalls.

refs.title: Spiced bottles 1: carbonate the keg for a medium sparkle
body: 1. Target: about 2.4 to 2.5 volumes of CO2 in the bottle. A picnic-tap fill loses a few tenths, so the keg needs about 2.8 volumes.
2. Chill the keg to about 38 F.
3. Set the regulator to 14 to 15 psi and hold it there for 7 to 10 days so the cider fully takes up the gas.
4. If the keg has been sitting cold at 20 psi it is over the target (about 3.3 volumes). Set the regulator to 15 psi and pull the relief valve once a day for a few days.
5. If the keg has been at 20 psi at room temperature (about 2.2 to 2.3 volumes), chill it and hold at 15 psi for a week.
6. Pressure only means something with temperature: 15 psi at 38 F is not the same as 15 psi at 60 F.

refs.title: Spiced bottles 2: bench trial the four tinctures
body: 1. Tinctures: allspice, cinnamon, cloves and anise seed, each in vodka. Strain each one through a coffee filter so no bits end up in the bottle (bits make a carbonated bottle gush).
2. Gear: a 1 mL syringe or dropper, a measuring cylinder, five glasses, a notebook.
3. Pour four 100 mL samples of cold cider from the keg, one per spice.
4. Add that spice's tincture in steps of 0.05 to 0.1 mL (1 to 2 drops), stir gently and taste after each step. Go smallest with cloves and anise; they take over fast.
5. Write down the dose where each spice tastes right on its own, in mL per 100 mL.
6. Pour a fresh 100 mL sample and build the blend: start each spice at half its solo dose, taste, then nudge one spice at a time.
7. Write down the final blend in mL per 100 mL for each of the four. That is the recipe.
8. Taste the samples cold and with their fizz. Warm, flat cider makes spice read stronger than it will in the bottle.

refs.title: Spiced bottles 3: scale the recipe up to the bottle
body: 1. Measure the bottle first: fill one with water to an inch below the stopper and pour it into a measuring jug. Swing-tops of this shape are usually 500 mL or 1 L, so do not assume 750 mL.
2. Multiply each dose by the bottle volume divided by 100: times 5 for 500 mL, times 7.5 for 750 mL, times 10 for 1 L.
3. Example: 0.3 mL cinnamon per 100 mL becomes 1.5 mL in a 500 mL bottle, 2.25 mL in a 750 mL bottle, or 3 mL in a 1 L bottle.
4. Add the four scaled doses together to get one blend dose per bottle.
5. Premix the blend for the whole run in a small jar: each spice's per-bottle amount times the number of bottles, plus one bottle's worth extra. Then every bottle gets the same single measured dose.
6. The half keg holds about 2.5 gallons (about 9.5 L): roughly 18 bottles at 500 mL, 12 at 750 mL or 9 at 1 L.
7. Fill one test bottle first, chill it for a day, and taste it before doing the rest. Adjust the blend if needed.
8. Keep sugar out of the blend. Any yeast left in the cider could ferment it in the bottle and build too much pressure.

refs.title: Spiced bottles 4: bottling day with the picnic tap and tubing
body: 1. Gear: picnic tap, a length of tubing that fits snugly inside the tap's spout (usually 3/8 inch outer diameter; take the tap to the brew shop) cut long enough to reach the bottom of the bottle, Star San, the syringe, the premixed blend, towels and a tray.
2. Get the keg as cold as the fridge allows.
3. Sanitize the bottles, stoppers and gaskets, the tubing, the tap and the syringe. Replace any gasket that is cracked or stiff.
4. Chill the wet bottles in the freezer for 20 to 30 minutes. Cold glass foams far less.
5. Shut off the gas, pull the relief valve to vent the keg, set the regulator to 2 to 3 psi and turn the gas back on.
6. Put the measured blend dose in the bottom of each bottle.
7. Push the tubing into the tap spout, rest its end on the bottom of a tilted bottle, and open the tap all the way. A half-open tap foams.
8. Fill gently from the bottom. When foam reaches the lip, close the tap and pull the tube out. That leaves about an inch of headspace.
9. Clamp the swing-top down straight away, onto the foam, so there is little air under the stopper.
10. Too foamy: colder bottles, or drop the pressure by 1 psi. Flow too slow: raise it by 1 psi.
11. Turn each bottle over once, gently, to mix in the spice. Label it with the blend and the date.
12. Store the bottles cold and upright and drink them within a month or two.
13. Put the keg back to its normal pressure and rinse the tap and tubing the same day.

card.status: Breeding is under way with your son. A few males died off and some crickets were lost to low humidity. The aim for now is simply to see whether you can breed them.

next.text: Buy more adult males

think.text: For humidity, a damp (not wet) laying dish and fresh vegetable slices add moisture without open water. Keep the air holes, since still, wet air grows mold.
A small hygrometer in one tub would tell you whether a change is working.
Keep new store-bought males apart for about a week before mixing them in, in case the batch is sick.

refs.title: Fight trials, from your breeding guide
body: Give each male at least 3 days alone first. Crickets kept in a crowd act like losers; time alone brings their aggression back.
Pair males that are close in weight. Let both settle with the divider in, then lift it.
If they ignore each other, tickle their antennae with a soft brush or grass stem.
Score each fight 0 to 4: 0 ignored each other, 1 antenna fencing, 2 jaws spread, 3 jaws locked, 4 wrestling.
The loser is the one that first avoids contact, runs, or stops chirping. Stop the fight the moment one backs off.
At most one fight per male per day.

refs.title: Key numbers
body: Hold the tubs at 82 to 88°F. Past 95°F is dangerous.
Eggs hatch in about 13 days at 86°F.
Females lay from about 8 to 10 days old as adults.
About 12 weeks per generation.

recipes.title: Soba noodle soup with mushroom dashi
recipes.note: Serves about 4. Start the dashi the night before, or at least 2 hours ahead.

sections.title: Dashi
items: 1 packed cup dried bonito flakes (1/2 oz)

sections.title: Soup
items: 6 scallions, thinly sliced, whites and greens kept separate

sections.title: Steps
items: Steep: put the water, kombu and dried shiitakes in a pot, cover, and leave overnight in the fridge (or at least 2 hours at room temperature).
Dashi: heat until it barely simmers, then take it off the heat. Stir in the bonito flakes and wait about 20 minutes, until they sink.
Strain through a fine sieve. You should have about 2 quarts. Cut the stems off the mushrooms and discard them, then slice the caps thinly. The kombu and bonito can be saved for a second batch.
Eggs, if using: lower into boiling water and cook 7 minutes. Drain, crack the shells all over with the back of a spoon, cover with cool water, then peel and halve.
Soba: boil in a medium pot until tender. Drain, rinse under running water while raking the noodles with your fingers until fully cool, and leave to drain.
In the same pot, cook the butter, walnuts, scallion whites and garlic over medium heat, stirring often, 3 to 5 minutes, until the butter browns and the nuts and garlic are just golden.
Stir in the sliced mushrooms to stop the browning. Add the soy sauce, maple syrup and pepper and cook about 1 minute, until absorbed.
Pour in the dashi, raise the heat to medium-high and bring to a simmer. Dissolve the miso in a little hot dashi in a small bowl, stir it into the pot, and take the pot off the heat.
Divide the noodles among bowls and ladle the soup over. Top with scallion greens and the eggs, and serve right away.
